abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations sample a continuum of conformations whose populations can reveal distinct protein structural states and substates as well as different ligand binding states. Determining which conformations belong to each state remains a central challenge in interpreting protein structural dynamics and ligand binding. Building on our framework for constructing free-energy surfaces from principal component projections of MD trajectories, we treat these surfaces as images. We adapt a method originally developed to segment cell nuclei in three-dimensional microscopy images and use the basin structure of the free-energy surface as the basis for clustering. We follow gradient flow toward free-energy minima and group neighboring regions by comparing the free energy along their shared boundaries with that within each region. When both regions contain resolved minima, we also test how far apart their cores are relative to their internal variation. Mapping the regions associated with the minima back to the original trajectories recovers the conformational ensemble in each state or substate and allows us to select a representative conformation directly from the simulation. We applied the method to conformational changes in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and the leucine transporter LeuT, and to the binding conformations sampled by a small-molecule drug interacting with the PP2A scaffold PR65. By combining statistical mechanics with computer vision, this approach provides a structural interpretation of how sampled conformational populations are organized
